blurb: Why models make things up, how to reduce it, and what interpretability research has found inside them.

cards.title: Fluent but wrong

steps.p: Pretraining rewards predicting likely text, not true text. Plausible-sounding falsehoods score fine.
Many evaluations give no credit for "I don't know", so models learn that a confident guess has better expected score.
Facts seen only a few times in training are stored weakly, and the model fills gaps with plausible patterns.

cards.aside: A hallucination is not a bug in one place; it is what next-token prediction does without grounding.

cards.q: A 2025 OpenAI paper argued one key cause of hallucination is that evaluations…
options: Reward guessing over admitting uncertainty, like tests with no penalty for wrong answers
cards.why: Incentives to guess. On a test where blanks score zero and guesses sometimes score, guessing wins. The paper proposed crediting appropriate abstention.

cards.q: Which is a model more likely to hallucinate?
options: The birth year of an obscure local politician
cards.why: The obscure fact. Facts that appear rarely in training data are poorly memorized, but the model still produces a confident-sounding answer.

cards.title: In 2023, US lawyers were fined for submitting a court brief citing cases that ChatGPT had invented.
cards.detail: In Mata v. Avianca, the judge found six cited decisions did not exist. The lawyers had even asked ChatGPT whether the cases were real, and it said yes.

cards.statement: Hallucinations only happen on obscure topics.
cards.why: False. They are more common there, but models also invent citations, quotes, URLs and numbers about well-known subjects, especially when asked for specifics.

cards.statement: OpenAI reported that GPT-4's pretrained base model was better calibrated about its confidence than the model after post-training.
cards.why: True. The GPT-4 technical report showed the base model's confidence matched its accuracy well, and post-training reduced that calibration.

cards.title: Practical defenses

steps.p: Give the model the source material, through search or RAG, and ask it to answer only from that.
Explicitly permitting abstention reduces confident guessing.
Ask for quotes supporting each claim, then check the quotes. A claim without a quote is suspect.

cards.aside: None of these is perfect, but together they cut error rates sharply.

cards.q: Which instruction most directly helps you catch hallucinations in a summary of a document?
options: "Quote the sentence from the document that supports each claim"
cards.why: Demand evidence. Quotes can be checked against the source in seconds, and a claim with no matching quote is a red flag.

cards.statement: A more fluent and detailed answer is more likely to be true.
cards.why: False. Fluency and detail are what the model is best at regardless of truth. Specific-sounding details are exactly what hallucinations look like.

options: Sampling several answers and checking whether they agree
cards.why: Consistency. Facts the model really knows tend to come out the same each time. Invented details vary between samples.

cards.title: Meta's "Chain-of-Verification" reduced hallucinations by having the model fact-check itself in separate steps.
cards.detail: The model drafts an answer, writes verification questions, answers each independently — without seeing the draft — then revises. Independence keeps it from repeating its own mistakes.

cards.title: Check numbers and names
cards.body: Hallucinations cluster in specifics: figures, dates, citations, names and URLs. Those are also the easiest things to verify quickly.
cards.challenge: Next time you use AI output at work, verify every number and citation in it before sending.

cards.title: Reverse-engineering a network

steps.p: Individual neurons often respond to several unrelated things — say, legal text and DNA — which makes them hard to interpret.
Models represent far more concepts than they have neurons by spreading each concept across many neurons in overlapping patterns.
Sparse autoencoders decompose activations into many more "features", each firing rarely and often matching one clear concept.

cards.aside: The goal: describe what a model computes in human-understandable parts.

cards.statement: Each neuron in a large language model typically represents one clean, understandable concept.
cards.why: False. Most neurons are polysemantic, responding to mixtures of unrelated concepts. That is why researchers look for features rather than neurons.

options: Representing more features than they have neurons by overlapping them
cards.why: Compression. If features rarely occur together, they can share neurons with little interference, letting a model pack in many more concepts.

cards.title: Anthropic made Claude believe it was the Golden Gate Bridge by amplifying one internal feature.
cards.detail: In May 2024, researchers found a feature for the bridge and turned it up. The resulting "Golden Gate Claude" steered nearly every conversation toward the bridge and even described itself as it.

cards.q: Anthropic's 2024 "Scaling Monosemanticity" work found millions of features in Claude 3 Sonnet, including…
options: Abstract features, such as for code bugs or deception, that work across languages and images
cards.why: Abstract, multilingual, multimodal features. The same feature might fire for a concept in English, French, or an image of it.

cards.q: A sparse autoencoder is trained to…
options: Rebuild a model's activations from a small number of active features out of a large dictionary
cards.why: Sparse reconstruction. Forcing only a few features to be active at once encourages each feature to capture one meaningful direction.

cards.title: Tracing a thought

steps.p: Researchers trace how features connect across layers to produce a specific answer.
Asked for the capital of the state containing Dallas, a model was seen to represent "Texas" internally before outputting "Austin".
When writing rhyming poetry, models were found to pick the rhyming word before writing the line that leads to it.

cards.aside: From Anthropic's 2025 work "On the Biology of a Large Language Model".

cards.q: When writing a rhyming couplet, interpretability research found Claude…
options: Picked words purely one at a time
Chose the rhyming word in advance and wrote the line to reach it
cards.why: Planning ahead. Despite generating one token at a time, the model held a target word internally — evidence that next-token prediction can involve planning.

cards.statement: Adding a vector to a model's activations can change its behavior without any retraining.
cards.why: True — activation steering. Adding a direction for a concept, such as a sentiment or topic, shifts outputs toward it during inference.

options: A simple classifier trained on a model's activations to test what information they contain
cards.why: A test for encoded information. If a simple linear probe can read, say, "is this statement true?" from activations, that information is readily represented there.

cards.title: Models appear to encode truth and falsehood along a simple direction in their activations.
cards.detail: Research such as "The Geometry of Truth" (2023) found that true and false statements separate along a linear direction, and that shifting along it can flip how the model treats a statement.

cards.statement: Interpretability research can already fully explain how frontier models make their decisions.
cards.why: False. Researchers can trace specific behaviors, but current methods capture only part of the computation. Full understanding of a frontier model remains far off.
